title: Pink, hot, electric: Bidirectional charging for the sauna - electrive.com
content:
Infrastructure
In Skellefteå, Sweden, energy provider Skellefteå Kraft is testing how a pink sauna can be powered by electricity from electric vehicle batteries. The unusual project showcases the potential of bidirectional charging.
The pink Crystal Sauna in Skellefteå can be heated using electricity from electric vehicle batteries.
Image: Studio Bigert & Bergström
It is pink, mirrored and shaped like a lithium crystal. The new “Crystal Sauna” in Skellefteå in northern Sweden looks a little like Barbie’s Dreamhouse for electric cars. Except this time, Ken is unlikely to be hanging out at the beach with his board – he is outside plugging in the EV.
The walk-in art installation stands in the so-called Wasteland, a former industrial site in Ursviken. Created as part of Society EXPO 2026, it is now a permanent installation owned by the municipality of Skellefteå and can be booked regularly. Energy is central to the design. The exterior takes its shape from a lithium crystal – the metal that plays a key role in today’s dominant lithium-ion batteries. Its façade consists of around 280 prisms clad in titanium-coated, pink mirrored panels. More than 140 laser-cut metal plates and over 3,500 screws went into its construction.
Inside, the futuristic crystal gives way to a cave-like space. Wood and a hand-forged sauna stove recall early human settlements and the harnessing of fire. The design thus draws a line from humanity’s first use of fire to the modern traction battery.
Bidirectional charging powers sauna from EV battery
For electric mobility enthusiasts, however, the most interesting aspect is how the sauna gets its energy. In the “Vehicle-to-Sauna” project, energy provider Skellefteå Kraft is testing a system that allows an electric vehicle battery to power the Crystal Sauna and the surrounding park. The installation can also draw energy from stationary batteries. The initiators describe it as the world’s first battery-powered sauna.
Behind the unusual use case is the familiar principle of bidirectional charging. A traction battery not only stores energy for driving but can also supply it elsewhere. Depending on the application, it can power a building (Vehicle-to-Home, V2H) or feed electricity back into the grid (Vehicle-to-Grid, V2G). The electric car thus becomes more than just a consumer: it can also serve as a mobile energy storage system.
The potential is considerable. In the future, millions of electric cars could absorb surplus wind and solar power and release it again when needed. The first business models for vehicle owners are already emerging. BMW and E.ON promise owners of a compatible iX3 earnings of up to €720 per year.
However, the technology is still far from widespread adoption.
Fragmented standards, a lack of interoperability, proprietary systems and – particularly in Germany – the slow rollout of smart metering systems are holding back progress. The Swedish experiment mainly serves as an example of the role electric vehicle batteries could play when they are not needed for driving.
While bidirectional charging has been discussed for years in terms of standards, business models and regulatory frameworks, the Swedes have simply switched on the sauna. That does not solve any of the challenges standing in the way of mass-market adoption, but it certainly gets people talking. And who knows? Perhaps the breakthrough needs less PowerPoint and more pink.

title: EcoPro BM upgrades Hungarian plant for NCM production - electrive.com
content:
EcoPro BM is adapting its cathode material plant in Debrecen, Hungary, to meet demand from European carmakers. An existing NCA production line will also produce high-nickel NCM material in the future. From late 2027, the South Korean manufacturer plans to supply the material to a German premium carmaker.
EcoPro BM’s cathode material plant in Debrecen, Hungary.
Image: EcoPro BM
EcoPro BM is investing around 40 billion won, equivalent to approximately 25 million euros, to upgrade its production facility in Debrecen. The company will convert a production line originally designed for NCA cathode material so that it can also manufacture NCM material. EcoPro BM has already ordered the necessary equipment.
NCM production itself is not new to the plans for the site. When the plant opened
in late 2025, EcoPro BM
said it would produce both high-nickel NCA and NCM cathode materials in Debrecen. The latest investment now confirms those plans for a specific customer project. From the fourth quarter of 2027, the plant will supply material with a nickel content of more than 90 per cent to a German premium car manufacturer. The customer has not been named, although BMW also produces vehicles in Debrecen.
EcoPro BM’s plant features three production lines with a combined annual capacity of 54,000 tonnes, sufficient for the batteries of around 600,000 electric cars. Following the ramp-up of the first line in June, the second is set to follow in September. For 2026, a production volume of around 10,000 tonnes is planned, increasing to 30,000 tonnes in 2027. In the long term, the site could expand further: at the groundbreaking in 2023, EcoPro BM had outlined a future capacity of 108,000 tonnes per year.
The EcoPro Group has established several stages of the production process at the approximately 440,000-square-metre site. EcoPro Innovation can supply 8,000 tonnes of lithium hydroxide per year, while EcoPro AP provides oxygen and nitrogen, among other materials, for the production process.
Samsung SDI
, which produces battery cells in the Hungarian town of Göd, is already set to source cathode material from Debrecen.
The new project with a German premium car manufacturer will further expand EcoPro BM’s European customer base. The company also wants to make its raw material supply more independent. Among other sources, it plans to procure nickel through the group’s BNSI smelting project in Indonesia. This is expected to improve supply security and its cost position – both important factors as European car manufacturers increasingly regionalise and secure their battery supply chains. At the same time, EcoPro BM needs to stabilise the still-young Hungarian site financially. Higher production volumes and better capacity utilisation are expected to bring the Hungarian subsidiary to quarterly profitability in the second half of 2026.

title: Anthro Energy breaks ground on electrolyte factory in Kentucky - electrive.com
content:
Anthro Energy has begun construction of its first commercial electrolyte factory in the US state of Kentucky. From late 2027, the facility will produce up to 12,000 tonnes of polymer electrolyte per year – enough for battery cells with a total capacity of up to 25 GWh. The technology could also be used in semi-solid and solid-state batteries in the future.
Anthro Energy is building an electrolyte factory in Louisville with an annual capacity of 12,000 tons.
Image: Anthro Energy
With the groundbreaking ceremony in Louisville, Anthro Energy has moved a project first announced in 2024 into the construction phase. The company describes the facility as the first US-owned and operated advanced electrolyte factory in the United States. Once construction is complete, Anthro plans to commission the plant in phases, with commercial production scheduled to begin in late 2027. The project is expected to create around 110 permanent jobs.
The factory will have an annual production capacity of approximately 12,000 tonnes of electrolyte. According to Anthro, this would be enough to support up to 25 GWh of lithium-ion cell production. The company sees potential applications in electric vehicles, stationary storage systems, consumer electronics, robotics and the defence sector. From the outset, Anthro plans to use only materials that are not subject to US regulations concerning so-called Foreign Entities of Concern (FEOC), with the aim of establishing a domestic supply source for a key battery cell component.
Polymer electrolyte could bridge the gap to solid-state batteries
Anthro’s proprietary Proteus platform is a key technological focus. The polymer electrolyte is initially processed as a liquid during cell production before solidifying. This allows the material to penetrate the anode and cathode in a similar way to conventional liquid electrolytes, while the subsequent phase transition is expected to improve the cell’s mechanical stability and safety.
For Anthro, the approach has another advantage: the Proteus platform can be integrated into existing lithium-ion cell production processes with relatively minor adjustments. However, the new factory will not produce Proteus exclusively. It will initially manufacture various electrolyte formulations, with the share of Proteus potentially increasing as customer validation progresses.
Anthro also sees the technology as a potential bridge to semi-solid and solid-state batteries. One of the main challenges for solid-state batteries remains the cost-effective mass production of high-performance cells with a long service life. Since Anthro’s polymer electrolyte can initially be processed as a liquid and only solidifies inside the cell, the technology could help overcome some of these manufacturing hurdles. Whether the approach will prove viable on an industrial scale, however, remains to be seen.
Plans for the Louisville facility have been known since autumn 2024
. At the time, the US Department of Energy selected Anthro Energy for a $24.9 million grant under the Infrastructure Investment and Jobs Act. The plans already envisaged an annual capacity of 12,000 tonnes, sufficient to support around 25 GWh of battery cell production. The US Department of Energy has since approved the project for implementation. Anthro has also received tax credits totalling $18.4 million under the 48C Advanced Energy Project Tax Credit Programme.
The Louisville site is located in the US ‘Battery Belt’, putting it close to numerous existing and planned battery cell and vehicle plants. According to CEO and co-founder David Mackanic, around 70 per cent of current US battery production is within a twelve-hour drive. This would allow the facility to supply US-made electrolytes to both conventional lithium-ion battery manufacturers and producers of next-generation cells in the future.

title: LG Energy Solution North America Head on Battery Market Pivot
content:
Battery Manufacturing
Industry Outlook
Battery Applications
Interviews
LGES North America President Bob Lee explains how Michigan plant balances EV and ESS production amid shifting demand, data center pushback, and emerging chemistries.
August 24, 2026
9 Min Read
The LGES facility in Lansing, MI, officially began production of LFP cells for energy storage systems on August 18, 2026.
M. Anderson / Battery TEchnology
At a Glance
Solid-state batteries will reach consumer electronics a decade before EVs due to manufacturing scalability challenges
AI data centers create unique battery opportunities due to dramatic power swings from compute cluster operations
LG is piloting sodium-ion for stationary storage while developing lithium-metal-rich chemistries for EVs
When Bob Lee, President of LG Energy Solution North America, discusses the company's newly operational Lansing, Michigan battery manufacturing facility, he frames it not merely as another addition to the continent's growing production capacity, but as a strategic response to fundamental market volatility.
In a news conference at the newly in-production plant on August 18, 2026, Lee—alongside Devon Wilson, LG's VP of Sales for grid-scale ESS energy storage division—outlined how the facility has evolved from its original conception as a dedicated EV battery plant into what may be the industry's most adaptable large-scale battery manufacturing operation in North America.
Devon Wilson (l) and Bob Lee talk to reporters at the event marking the start of production of ESS cells at the LGES Lansing facility on August 18, 2026. Credit: M. Anderson / Battery Technology
The transformation reflects Lee's assessment of market realities: automotive programs carry long development cycles and uncertain volume projections, while energy storage systems offer more stable revenue patterns and are experiencing structural demand growth driven by grid modernization needs. LG has repositioned the Lansing facility to balance both opportunities while maintaining the flexibility to shift production as markets evolve.
Related:
LG Energy Solution Opens First US Large-Scale LFP Battery Plant for Energy Storage
Key insights: From AI data centers to solid-state timelines
Lee's perspective on emerging applications and technologies offers a reality check on several topics dominating industry discussions. On artificial intelligence infrastructure, he confirmed that AI data centers represent a distinct ESS opportunity due to their unique power consumption patterns—compute clusters that activate and deactivate simultaneously create dramatic load swings that batteries can smooth far more effectively than conventional generation.
However, Lee emphasized responsible development: "I think now we've gotten better at responsible data center development, so that you need to make sure that the community is not impacted in terms of things like the water and power." Wilson noted that while AI facilities generate attention, "the lion's share of our growth is just based on basic fundamentals of retiring legacy thermal generation assets."
On solid-state batteries—a technology that has attracted billions in investment and countless optimistic timelines—Lee offered a sobering assessment: "You will see that in your smartphones probably a decade before you would ever see it in EVs." The challenge isn't laboratory performance but manufacturing scalability at the large form factors required for automotive and energy storage applications.
Meanwhile, LG is actively piloting sodium-ion technology for stationary storage, maintaining strategic optionality as supply chain dynamics evolve. "We want to have all those options open," Wilson explained, though LFP remains the optimal chemistry for most current ESS projects.
Related:
How LG Energy Solution Navigates North America’s Unsettled Market Dynamics
Another emerging opportunity: battery integration with EV charging infrastructure, which Lee identified as "one of our future growth segments." By co-locating batteries with charging stations, operators can dramatically reduce electrical infrastructure buildout costs—a practical solution LG is beta testing with charging hardware manufacturers.
Originally launched as part of the Ultium joint venture with General Motors, LG has since assumed 100% ownership and fundamentally restructured the facility's mission. The plant now operates with roughly equal capacity dedicated to EV batteries and energy storage systems, with Toyota serving as the anchor automotive customer while multiple ESS clients utilize the facility's production capabilities.
In a major pivot away from its earlier EV plans, GM is sold its half of the Lansing facility to LG in 2024. Credit: GMpivoting away from the Ultium cells that were the centerpiece of its EV strategy.
The technical challenges of converting EV-focused production lines to accommodate different chemistries and form factors are substantial. The shift to lithium iron phosphate (LFP) chemistry for energy storage required significant process modifications.
Related:
GM & LG Energy Solution Strengthen US EV Supply Chain with LFP Batteries
"[With] LFP, usually the coating loading is thicker, so you need to have more roll press to compress, and then there's slight differences in the manufacturing process itself," Lee noted. "So you do need to put in some new equipment and validate that in order to build batteries from one another."
Beyond chemistry changes, the Lansing facility is preparing to produce both LFP pouch cells and LFP prismatic cells—a capability requiring additional line investments but leveraging LG's historical experience with multiple cell formats.
Lee emphasized that LG's long tenure provides crucial institutional knowledge: "We've been in the battery industry for a long time. We've actually had experience with LFP in the past as we moved on to focus on NMC recently. So I think this plant is a great example of how fast we were able to put in the capacity."
LFP cell production at the Lansing facility. Credit: LGES
The company claims to be the first major manufacturer to successfully execute this type of large-scale conversion, positioning the Lansing facility as what Lee termed a "mother plant"—a testing ground for new technologies and processes before broader deployment across LG's North American manufacturing network.
AI data centers create specialized requirements and community concerns
Artificial intelligence computing facilities represent an emerging ESS application with unique technical demands. Unlike traditional data centers with relatively steady power consumption, AI facilities experience dramatic load swings as compute clusters activate and deactivate simultaneously.
"AI data centers are usually unique in which it's clusters of compute that all get turned on at once and then get turned off at once," Wilson explained. "So if you look at the energy demand, it swings up and down, and so while the overall energy need can be met, those swings are problematic."
Battery systems address this challenge through rapid response capabilities that conventional generation cannot match, smoothing load profiles to prevent grid disruption. This requires careful hardware selection—including specific cell chemistries and power conversion equipment—integrated with sophisticated control software.
However, Lee acknowledged that data center deployments face legitimate community concerns that the industry must address responsibly, noting that Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer had addressed these issues in her remarks at the event.
"In general, a lot of people are concerned about water not being available in the intervening area, or power either not being available or prices going up," Lee explained. "So I think now we've gotten better at responsible data center development. I think municipalities and developers are [also] getting much better at doing that.”
Lee emphasized LG's commitment to supporting only responsible data center buildouts that address infrastructure and environmental impacts on surrounding communities.
EV charging infrastructure emerges as growth segment
Battery integration with electric vehicle charging infrastructure represents what Lee identified as "one of our future growth segments for our ESS business." The primary challenge in deploying high-speed charging isn't the charging hardware itself but rather the electrical infrastructure required to deliver power to charging locations.
"There's a lot of opportunities to use batteries, so you don't have to build out all the infrastructure," Wilson noted. "You can reduce those costs by having batteries globally."
LG is conducting beta testing with charging station hardware manufacturers to develop optimized battery system specifications for this application, which differs from both grid-scale containerized solutions and behind-the-meter installations.
Chemistry roadmap balances application needs with manufacturing reality
LG's approach to emerging and alternative battery chemistries reflects careful assessment of both application requirements and manufacturing readiness—a pragmatic stance that distinguishes hype from near-term commercial viability.
For stationary storage applications, where weight and volumetric energy density matter far less than cost, safety, and cycle life, LFP currently offers the optimal balance. "We always look to apply the right chemistry for the application, and stationary is very different than an EV application where weight and density doesn't matter as much," Wilson explained. "LFP is a really great choice when you talk about stationary storage ESS."
However, LG is actively piloting sodium-ion technology to maintain strategic optionality as supply chain dynamics and project economics evolve. The company expects sodium-ion may prove advantageous for certain project types or operational profiles while LFP continues serving the majority of applications.
For automotive applications requiring higher energy density, LG is developing lithium-metal-rich (LMR) and mid-nickel chemistries focused on the affordability that customers increasingly demand. "Those are products that we're working very closely right now with our customers because they're driving toward more affordability," Lee noted.
These advanced lithium-ion chemistries can be accommodated within current manufacturing infrastructure. "If you look at that kind of parameter, I would say we would, in general, be able to produce that in the same plant with some adjustments to our equipment," Lee explained.
Solid-state technology, despite decades of development attention and substantial industry investment, faces a fundamentally different timeline. Lee offered a sobering assessment that challenges the optimistic projections often heard at industry conferences: "You will see that in your smartphones probably a decade before you would ever see it in EVs."
The core challenge is manufacturing scalability rather than laboratory performance. "The problem with solid state is large scale production," Lee explained. "It has very good energy density, so if you're making it in small form formats, you should be able to get that. But if you're starting to make it in very large form factors, it's proven that those companies struggle."
Lee expects initial commercial applications in consumer electronics or highly specialized use cases before solid-state technology achieves the scale required for EVs or energy storage systems. "So yes, it's interesting technology. We're researching. We've invested in companies, but at the same time, I think we have to stay clear-eyed in terms of how fast we can get to scale."
Strategic positioning for market uncertainty
LG's investment trajectory in Michigan—spanning from the 2012 Holland plant launch through multiple presidential administrations—demonstrates long-term commitment despite policy volatility. The Lansing facility's design as a large-scale, single-building operation with diverse customer base and chemistry flexibility positions the company to navigate continued market uncertainty.
Lee's confidence in the plant's medium-term outlook centers on customer strength and technology positioning: "Toyota is one of our main customers here. I would say Toyota is a very strong customer, so I have very high confidence in their ability to be a good customer and produce good vehicles and ultimately sell vehicles into the market."
For the broader battery manufacturing industry, LG's Lansing facility offers a template for managing the transition period as markets mature and technology evolves—demonstrating that manufacturing flexibility and systems-level expertise may prove as valuable as raw production capacity in navigating the decade ahead.

title: UPS Invests US$2bn to Speed Up Global Supply Chains
content:
UPS Invests US$2bn to Speed Up Global Supply Chains
Prioritise Us
on Google
UPS is looking to help businesses navigate shifting trade routes, evolving regulations and supply chain uncertainty with greater flexibility (Credit: UPS)
UPS EVP Kate Gutmann details a US$2bn network investment across Europe, Asia-Pacific and the Americas to speed customer shipments
UPS has confirmed ongoing investments equating to more than US$2bn across its International, Healthcare and Supply Chain Solutions businesses, running from 2024 through to 2028.
This investment programme is designed to help customers navigate shifting trade routes, evolving regulations and supply chain uncertainty, with greater flexibility and connectivity across key global markets.
For senior supply chain leaders managing
cross-border complexity
, the announcement signals where one of the world's largest logistics providers is putting its capital, and which capabilities it expects customers to need most over the next two years.
New hubs anchor the expansion
Three new facilities sit at the centre of the announcement: a hub at Clark Airport in the Philippines, due to open in the fourth quarter of 2026; a new Canadian facility in Barrie, Ontario, opening in 2027; and a new air hub at Hong Kong International Airport, scheduled for 2028.
These sit alongside recent investments in healthcare and other strategic segments, including high-tech, automotive and
industrial manufacturing
These investments allow us to bring air, ground, brokerage and distribution together in one solution, with fewer handoffs, more end-to-end control and less complexity.
Kate Gutmann, Executive Vice President and President of International, Healthcare and Supply Chain Solutions, UPS
In June 2026, UPS confirmed a US$48m investment in 27 temperature-controlled freight
cross-dock facilities worldwide
, built to move biologics and other temperature-sensitive medicines between air and ground networks without breaking the cold chain. In May 2026, UPS separately invested around US$50m in network capabilities for automotive and industrial manufacturers, including the expansion of its North American Air Freight service to and from Mexico for the first time.
Kate Gutmann, Executive Vice President and President of International, Healthcare and Supply Chain Solutions at UPS, says the goal is to reduce complexity for customers handling sensitive shipments.
What customers gain from the network
UPS says its global network is built to give customers greater visibility and control of their logistics, through:
end-to-end cold-chain capabilities, positioning UPS as the world's leading provider of complex healthcare logistics
the fastest integrated ground network in Europe, covering every address on the continent, with Saturday delivery in eight leading markets
one of the broadest Asia-Pacific networks of IATA CEIV Pharma-certified facilities for moving high-value, time-sensitive shipments
automatic Saturday ground residential delivery in Canada, the only integrated carrier to offer this as standard
expanded North American Air Freight capabilities, including new time-definite heavy air freight service to and from Mexico.
A customer view from Anker
UPS points to Anker, a global smart hardware
technology company
, as an example of how the investments translate into practice. As Anker expanded its manufacturing footprint, the company faced new trade requirements and growing market complexity.
Adam Liu, Chief Supply Chain Officer at Anker, credits UPS with combining transportation, brokerage and trade expertise to help the company manage that growth with confidence, rather than simply moving products from one location to another.
Another recent investment by UPS includes opening a new operation centre in Taiwan. (Credit: UPS)
Why this matters for supply chain leaders
The investments arrive as automation, geopolitical shifts and evolving regulation continue to pressure global supply chains. Elsewhere in its network, UPS reports automation now covers more than two-thirds (67.5%) of its facilities in North America, part of a wider push to increase visibility through technologies such as
RFID sensing
For supply chain leaders assessing logistics partners, the scale and geographic spread of the investment, spanning Asia-Pacific, Europe and North America, points to where UPS expects sustained demand: healthcare, high-tech, automotive and industrial manufacturing.
Key partner cited: Anker
Anker is a global smart hardware technology company known for charging, audio and smart home products, sold across more than 100 countries. Adam Liu serves as Chief Supply Chain Officer, overseeing the company's international logistics and trade operations as it scales manufacturing capacity. Anker relies on UPS's integrated transportation, brokerage and trade expertise to manage cross-border complexity during periods of rapid growth.

title: BYD opens orders for its new flagship EV with over 1,000 km of range for under $40,000
content:
Peter Johnson
| Aug 24 2026 - 8:24 am PT
opened orders for the Great Han, its new flagship electric sedan that can drive over 1,000 km (621 mi) on a single charge, starting at under $40,000.
BYD opens orders for the flagship Great Han EV
The Great Han, or Da Han as it’s called in China, is the first D-segment flagship sedan under BYD’s Dynasty family.
a sneak peek
of the new full-size sedan in June after it was revealed in the batch of new energy vehicles approved for sale by China’s MIIT (Ministry of Industry and Information Technology).
Lu Tian, the general manager of BYD’s Dynasty series, confirmed last month that the Great Han would be revealed in full at the Chengdu Motor Show, teasing that “more surprises await.”
Tian also confirmed the electric sedan will offer a CLTC driving range of up to 1,008 km (626 miles) on a single charge.
BYD opened pre-orders for the new Great Han at the event, starting at just 249,900 yuan, or about $37,200.
BYD Great Han (Da Han) flagship electric sedan (Soure: Lu Tian)
The flagship sedan is available in three variants with single and all-wheel drive powertrains. Two rear-wheel drive (RWD) options are available: Premium and Flagship, starting at 249,900 yuan ($37,2000) and 269,900 yuan ($40,200).
Both are powered by a single 370 kW (496 hp) motor and 102.326 kWh battery, providing a CLTC driving range of up to 1,008 km (626 miles).
The AWD variant adds a frton electric motor for a combined 570 kW (764 hp). Although it uses the same battery pack as the RWD variants, the AWD version has a CLTC range of 880 km (546 miles).
All Great Han variants are equipped with BYD’s Blade Battery 2.0 and Flash Charging technology. The setup enables vehicles equipped with the new batteries to recharge from 10% to 70% in just 5 minutes using 1,500 kW technology. For a full recharge (10% to 97%), it takes just 9 minutes.
Measuring 5,256 mm in length, 1,999 mm in width, and 1,510 mm in height, with a wheelbase of 3,130 mm, BYD’s flagship sedan is bigger than the Tesla Model S and Lucid Air. It’s closer in size to the long-wheelbase Mercedes S-Class.
Like the flagship Great Tang SUV, BYD said the sedan is loaded with premium standard features, including its DiSus-A dual chamber air suspension system, rear-wheel steering, and zero gravity front seats.
All Great Han variants are also equipped with BYD’s God’s Eye B smart driving system, offering ADAS features like Navigation on Autopilot and remote parking.
The new flagship sedan is part of BYD’s broader push into higher end segments following the Great Tang SUV and several new vehicles under its premium Denza brand.

title: Watch Tesla FSD v14 Lite drive over a giant log without stopping
content:
A Tesla owner posted dashcam footage of his car driving straight over a log lying across the road while running Full Self-Driving (FSD) v14.1 Lite, without braking or slowing down.
The clip has more than 800,000 views, and it adds to a growing list of problems we’ve documented with Tesla’s “Lite” version of FSD on older Hardware 3 cars.
In the video, posted by X user @donvarri on August 21, the car is on a wet, foggy rural road with the “Self-Driving” visualization active at 32 mph. A log sits across the lane. The Tesla runs right over it. No braking, no swerve.
“Mine drove over a log in the road it def wouldn’t have stopped,” the owner wrote. He later confirmed the car is a Hardware 3 vehicle running the latest v14.1 Lite build.
The problems with v14 Lite keep stacking up
FSD v14 Lite is a compressed version of the HW4 v14 model, squeezed onto HW3’s memory-constrained AI3 computer, which has 8GB of RAM and roughly one-eighth the bandwidth of the newer hardware. Tesla started rolling it out to Hardware 3 cars in June.
Since then, the reports haven’t been good.
Owners have documented HW3 computers overheating under the extra processing load, triggering an APP_w141_ECU_Thermal_Issue fault above 90°C, with some temperatures hitting 96°C. In several cases the system threw “red hands” and forced a disengagement, and a few computers shut down entirely and needed replacement. On top of that, drivers reported phantom braking, hesitation, and brake stuttering.
Tesla shipped v14.1 Lite partly to address the overheating. This log incident is on that supposedly improved build.
And the bigger issue hasn’t gone anywhere. HW3 simply can’t deliver the unsupervised autonomy Tesla sold, the company has admitted it has no clear plan to get there, and it sold roughly 4 million cars as “full self-driving capable” for as much as $15,000.
The complacency problem, in the driver’s own words
The replies quickly turned into a fight about whose fault it was. Several people told the owner he should have been watching the road and intervened.
His answer is the whole story: “2 things can be true I should have been paying attention but the car definitely should have stopped.”
That’s the trap with a Level 2 system that’s good most of the time. One commenter put the blame squarely on the driver: “No, YOU allowed that to happen for the opportunity to post a video, by failing to properly supervise.” The owner pushed back that he’s no Tesla hater, that he’s driven 70,000 miles, and that it’s the best car he’s ever owned.
But here’s the problem. The better FSD gets at routine driving, the more the driver relaxes. And that’s exactly when it plows over an obstacle a human would have caught from a hundred feet away. The system trains its own supervisor to stop supervising.
Electrek’s Take
Both things are true. He should have been paying attention, and the car should have stopped for a log in the middle of the road at 32 mph. Blaming the driver lets the system off the hook, and blaming the system ignores what supervision is for.
Top comment by Beario
I paid for autonomy on the two cars that we have with FSD. What we have is a system that we use sparingly on the highway on long trips. It CANNOT be trusted because it is not capable of doing what it was intended to do. The hardware just can't and now we are just shy of a hardware 5 which is 2 full hardware upgrades ahead. I fully do not expect Tesla to do anything as they will wait for the cars to disappear with time. The lawsuits pending in Europe are the right move and it most certainly should be done the same here. Tesla should be held accountable yesterday with lawsuits, not tomorrow.
I’ve been on the wrong end of this. Almost a decade ago I had a similar but less severe accident in a Model 3, and it still cost my insurers around $15,000 in suspension and frame repair. Hitting a solid log at 32 mph is a lot more violent than what I went through. I wouldn’t be surprised if this car ends up totaled once someone looks at the underbody.
To think that the driver would have done it on purpose is ridiculous.
The complacency issue is real, but it’s a design problem as much as a driver problem. Tesla keeps pushing more capable software onto hardware it already admitted can’t do the job, and the result is a system smooth enough to lull you and brittle enough to run over a log. HW3 owners paid for autonomy. What are they actually getting?

title: Tesla loses another top chip engineer to ex-Dojo startup DensityAI
content:
Fred Lambert
| Aug 24 2026 - 6:09 am PT
Tesla has lost another senior chip engineer to DensityAI, the AI hardware startup built out of its own former Dojo team. Shishuang Sun, who spent more than five years as a Tesla AI hardware architect on Dojo and the Autopilot computers, now lists his role as “Packaging and System Hardware” at DensityAI, starting in July.
This is not a junior loss. Sun left Tesla as Senior Director of AI Hardware Design — one of the people responsible for turning Tesla’s custom silicon into working systems, exactly the expertise Tesla needs as it stakes its valuation on in-house AI chips.
A Tesla chip veteran, twice over
Sun’s career traces the entire arc of Tesla’s in-house silicon ambition. According to his LinkedIn history, he first joined Tesla’s Autopilot hardware group during the Jim Keller era, when Tesla was assembling the team that would design its first Full Self-Driving computer and cut its dependence on Nvidia.
He left around the time that chapter wound down, spending just over two years at Waymo as a hardware engineering manager, where he ran the design verification, signal and power integrity, EMC, and PCB teams that make up the guts of self-driving hardware.
Then he came back. Sun rejoined Tesla in January 2021 as a principal engineer on AI hardware for both Dojo and Autopilot, and was promoted to Senior Director of AI Hardware Design in April 2025. His work covered IC packaging, vertical power modules, signal and power integrity, PCB design, and system thermal and mechanical engineering — the discipline of taking a chip design and making it survive in the real world.
The startup was built out of Tesla’s Dojo team
DensityAI is not a random competitor. As
we reported when Tesla shut Dojo down
in August 2025, the startup was founded by former Dojo chief Ganesh Venkataramanan, with roughly 20 members of Tesla’s supercomputer team following him out the door. Fellow Tesla veteran Bill Chang is CTO.
The company is building chips, hardware, and software for AI data centers aimed at automotive, robotics, and industrial customers — effectively the mission Tesla walked away from when it killed Dojo and shifted to Nvidia for training compute.
Losing packaging talent at the worst possible time
Sun’s specialty — advanced packaging and system integration — is the part of chipmaking that has become the industry’s real bottleneck. Getting the transistor design right is only half the job; getting power into the chip and heat out of it, at scale, is where high-performance AI silicon lives or dies.
Tesla is leaning on custom silicon harder than ever. It
taped out its long-delayed AI5 chip in April
, nearly two years behind Musk’s original timeline, with volume production not expected until mid-2027. AI6 is slated for Samsung’s 2nm process, which has hit yield problems, and Musk has floated a “Dojo 3” on top of that. On the manufacturing side, Tesla and SpaceX are pitching the
$20 billion-plus “Terafab” chip factory in Austin
Every one of those bets depends on people who can turn a tape-out into a shipping product — the packaging, power delivery, and thermal work that Sun did at Tesla for five years.
Electrek’s Take
DensityAI has now pulled in Tesla’s former Dojo leadership, roughly 20 of its engineers, and — a full year later — a sitting Senior Director of AI hardware, who appeared to be promoted into an exec role after the talent drain.
It shows continued bleeding, well after Tesla supposedly regrouped around AI5 and AI6. When a company pins its entire valuation on becoming an AI and robotics chip player, the steady loss of the people who actually build that hardware matters.
The irony is hard to miss. Tesla killed Dojo, watched the team spin up a competitor. Custom silicon is a people business before it’s a fab business, and right now the people are moving in one direction.

title: XPeng robotics raises $900M at $6.3B valuation for IRON robot push
content:
XPeng’s robotics business has raised over $900 million at a post-money valuation of more than $6.3 billion, the Chinese EV maker announced today. XPeng calls it the largest single-round private financing in the history of China’s embodied AI industry.
The round is meant to push XPeng’s IRON humanoid robot into mass production by the end of 2026 — a timeline that keeps the automaker ahead of Tesla’s stalling Optimus program.
A record raise, and a carve-out
The financing was led by IDG Capital, with participation from Gaorong Ventures and strategic backing from Tencent and Alibaba, according to XPeng.
The company frames the round as validation of its “leadership in Physical AI” and its “ability to scale production.” Of the $900 million-plus committed, roughly $600 million comes from external investors, with about $200 million from an XPeng subsidiary and $100 million from leadership.
The raise comes alongside a corporate restructuring. XPeng is spinning its robotics assets, IP, and staff into a standalone subsidiary over the next 18 months while retaining roughly 82% ownership, which keeps the unit consolidated on the group’s financial statements but gives it a separate market valuation. CEO He Xiaopeng took direct control of the robotics business in June 2026.
What IRON actually is
XPeng unveiled the next-generation IRON at its AI Day event in November 2025, where the robot’s fluid, human-like walk was so convincing that online viewers accused the company of hiding a person in a costume. He Xiaopeng responded by cutting open the robot’s leg on stage to reveal the wiring underneath.
The hardware is genuinely ambitious. IRON carries 76 degrees of freedom across its body and 21 in each hand, wrapped in what XPeng calls a “fully enclosed flexible lattice structure” — a synthetic skin meant to balance safety and a human-like appearance.
On the compute side, IRON runs three of XPeng’s in-house Turing AI chips delivering a combined 2,250 TOPS. That lets the company run its Physical AI foundation model directly on the robot, which XPeng says allows IRON to “autonomously perform complex tasks without remote operation.”
Rival humanoid demos are frequently teleoperated by humans off-camera, and XPeng is explicitly claiming on-device autonomy — a claim that will be worth scrutinizing once IRON is in customers’ hands rather than on a stage.
The manufacturing argument
Top comment by BCGeiger
This is why right now I wouldn't touch Tesla stock. Their cars are old with aged and increasingly second class technology. Sales are dropping because of it. Musk is betting the company on two things. Grok, which is an also-ran that almost nobody outside of X is using because it is massively worse than the top AI systems. And Optimus which is a decade or more behind the top systems from Chinese, European, or even other US companies. Musk's hat is out of rabbits. It's going to be a brutal few years for the markets and Musk.
Keep in mind that 1929 was almost exactly 100 years ago. History repeating and all that.
XPeng’s core pitch is that it can bring “automotive-grade quality standards and large-scale mass production” to humanoid robots by leaning on the supply chain and factories it built for EVs.
XPeng reported 103,295 vehicle deliveries in the second quarter of 2026, up 64.8% quarter-over-quarter, so the company is scaling actual hardware at volume right now. It says the robotics unit is targeting monthly capacity of more than 1,000 IRON units and has floated a goal of 1 million units by 2030.
The plan is for IRON to enter mass production by the end of 2026, starting inside XPeng’s own stores and campuses, before an official launch with deliveries in China and overseas markets in 2027.

title: Heybike launches low cost 28 MPH full-suspension moped-style e-bike
content:
Micah Toll
| Aug 24 2026 - 4:55 am PT
Heybike is expanding into a rather different corner of the e-bike market with the launch of the new Heybike Titan, a full-suspension, moped-style electric bike that can be had with either one or two batteries.
And perhaps just as importantly, Heybike is coming out swinging on price.
The new Titan
starts at $1,499
for the single-battery version, while the dual-battery model carries
an MSRP of $1,799
. Early-bird pricing knocks another $100 off each, bringing them down to $1,399 and $1,699, respectively.
That’s some pretty aggressive pricing for this style of bike, especially once you get into the dual-battery version.
But what do you get for that price?
The Titan is powered by a 750W rear hub motor rated for a claimed 1,500W of peak power and 65 Nm of torque. It ships configured as a Class 2 e-bike with a 20 mph (32 km/h) top speed, though Heybike says riders can use the company’s app to adjust the bike up to 28 mph (45 km/h).
The bike also carries UL 2849 certification, which covers the entire electrical system and is becoming increasingly important as more cities, retailers, landlords, and consumers pay attention to e-bike battery safety.
But the more interesting part of the Titan is probably its battery setup.
The single-battery model uses a 48V 15Ah battery, or 720 Wh, and Heybike claims up to 40 miles (64 km) of range. Opt for the dual-battery version and you’re effectively getting 1,440 Wh of capacity, with Heybike doubling its maximum range estimate to 80 miles (129 km).
As always, take those maximum range figures with the usual grain of salt. Riding a heavy moped-style e-bike at higher speeds and relying heavily on the throttle is going to chew through batteries much more quickly. Going full balls to the wall could leave you with half of that range, but the point is that dual batteries are definitely going to take you further, and so having the dual-battery option is a nice feature here.
There are
plenty of moped-style e-bikes and plenty of dual-battery e-bikes,
but the Venn diagram gets considerably smaller when you’re looking for a moped-style bike that combines dual batteries with actual front and rear suspension.
The Titan gets an 80mm-travel hydraulic front fork and 55mm of rear suspension travel, with the rear comprised of dual coil-over shocks as compared to the more common bicycle-style mono-shock setup. Add in those chunky 20 x 4-inch tires, and you’ve got the basic recipe for the increasingly popular mini-moto style of e-bike that prioritizes comfort, cruising, and a motorcycle-inspired riding experience.
Hydraulic brakes are included as well, and the bike has a 300 lb (136 kg) maximum payload rating. Heybike has even fitted rear footrests and describes the long saddle as “two-up ready,” though that same 300 lb payload limit is worth keeping in mind before inviting a friend aboard.
At 85 lb (38.4 kg) for the single-battery version and 93 lb (42.1 kg) with two batteries, nobody is going to confuse the Titan for a lightweight commuter. But that’s increasingly beside the point with this category. These bikes are basically designed to bring a bit of small-motorcycle swagger to an e-bike platform.
And that’s also what makes the Titan an interesting move for Heybike.
The company has traditionally focused much more heavily on conventional fat-tire commuters, folders, step-through bikes, and other mainstream value-oriented e-bikes. The Titan is a pretty clear attempt to reach into the youth-oriented, moped-style segment that has exploded in popularity.
In fact, Heybike isn’t exactly hiding that ambition. Its own marketing materials explicitly identify “trendsetters,” “teen cruisers,” and “parent buyers” among the Titan’s target audiences, while leaning heavily into the bike’s social, customizable and mini-moto image. There’s even a glow-in-the-dark sticker kit included for riders who want to personalize the bike.
That helps explain the aggressive pricing, too. Heybike appears to be trying to go past just adding another variation of an existing commuter here; the company is looking to enter a new part of the market and appears ready to buy itself some market share.
At $1,399 for an early single-battery Titan or $1,699 for the dual-battery version, Heybike is making a pretty compelling argument on the spec sheet. The latter in particular packs full suspension, hydraulic brakes, a 1,500W peak motor and nearly 1.5 kWh of battery into a price point where plenty of competing moped-style bikes still make you choose between range, suspension, or spending considerably more.
That said, we’ll have to see how the Titan rides before knowing whether that aggressive value translates from the spec sheet to the street. Compared to other new entrants to this market, like the
revamped Juiced Scrambler
, which is marginally more expensive but offers higher-end components and is designed to actually be pedalable, the Titan is going to have to demonstrate that it can offer a good ride and not just a good price. But for Heybike’s first serious swing at this increasingly crowded moped-style e-bike market, the company certainly isn’t easing its way in.

title: Cost savings top disaster prep in Japan solar-storage survey - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Battery storage is emerging as a financial tool for Japanese households rather than just a disaster-preparedness measure, according to a new survey of residential solar and storage prospects.
Brian Publicover
24 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Energy Storage
Only 19% of respondents to an August survey by iChoosr, a Japanese solar and battery group-purchasing platform, named disaster resilience as their reason for considering solar panels or home batteries, compared with 48% who cited reducing their electricity bills, the company said. The respondents were asked to select a single primary reason.
The survey covered 14,478 people across 24 prefectures who registered interest in installing solar panels or batteries through iChoosr’s “Minna no Ouchi ni Taiyoko” (“Solar for Everyone’s Home”) program between Feb. 25 and July 23. iChoosr said the results indicate that financial considerations are cited more often than disaster preparedness among respondents.
The finding comes as Japan’s original wave of residential feed-in tariff (FIT) contracts, which guaranteed fixed export payments for 10 years, continues to expire. The transition has also reshaped Japan’s utility-scale solar market as
legacy FIT projects approach expiry
and owners reassess revenue strategies. The Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry (METI) said approximately 530,000 residential solar installations, representing roughly 2 GW of capacity, left the FIT scheme in November and December 2019 alone.
Once a household’s FIT contract ends, export compensation typically falls well below the retail price of electricity, making it more economical for many households to store and consume their own solar power rather than sell it back to the grid, even as
Japan’s residential solar demand
continues to grow.
Other recent Japanese surveys have also found cost-related motivations ranking ahead of resilience among battery buyers and prospective buyers. A poll published in March by Goodfellows, a Japanese solar and battery marketplace operator, found that 51.9% of existing solar owners considering a battery cited electricity savings in 2025, up from 39.3% in 2022, while the share citing emergency power stayed close to 30% over the same period. A separate 2025 survey by ECODA, a Japanese residential solar and battery installer, found that 76% of respondents expected solar and battery systems to reduce electricity costs, against 49.1% who expected them to provide power during disasters. However, these surveys used different methodologies and sampled different populations, meaning their findings are not directly comparable to iChoosr’s results or to each other.
Resilience concerns in Japan trace in part to Typhoon Faxai, which made landfall in eastern Japan on Sept. 9, 2019. METI reported peak outages of approximately 930,000 households across the Tepco service area, including approximately 637,100 in Chiba prefecture, and Tepco said some households continued to rely on power-supply trucks and generators for weeks after the storm as repair crews worked to clear storm damage. A survey of 486 residential solar owners affected by the storm, conducted by the Japan Photovoltaic Energy Association (JPEA) and later cited by METI, found that 79.8% reported using their system’s independent-operation function to keep essential appliances such as refrigerators and lighting running during the outage.
iChoosr’s program pools demand from participating households so installers can bid competitively for the resulting volume, a model the company says lowers costs compared with individual, one-off installations. The company reports more than 110,000 cumulative household registrations in Japan since 2019 and says it has facilitated more than 10,000 installations, though it did not specify what share of registered households went on to install a system.
Japanese utilities are also beginning to draw on residential batteries for grid balancing rather than treating them purely as a household backup or self-consumption tool. Kyushu Electric Power has run a
demonstration project using Sharp home batteries
, remotely coordinating charging during periods of high solar output and discharging during tighter-supply periods. Industry analysts expect
Japan’s residential, commercial and industrial storage markets to keep expanding
as the country builds out a national virtual power plant (VPP) program, adding a further revenue stream and dispatch use case for battery-owning households beyond the FIT-driven economics described in the iChoosr survey.

title: AI platform aims to transform solar site assessment - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Learnewable uses AI-based insights to detail local solar opposition before developers invest time or energy in projects.
Anne Fischer
24 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Technology & Products
Software
Local opposition to solar energy comes in many forms, from neighbors who live near proposed large-scale installations, to organized groups and municipal boards who pass legislation banning utility scale projects. For the developer,
opposition equals risk
and risk reduces the bankability of projects.
Learnewable is a startup that offers developers an AI-based tool that provides risk assessments based on insights into local opposition to siting solar, battery energy storage, wind and even data centers. The company recently launched an interactive county-level map that uses those insights to show solar developers the social landscape before they begin the process of due diligence for a project.
The way it works is Learnewable gleans information on local sentiment, permitting, zoning, restriction and moratoria from public records, local news and social media. It then applies multiple AI tools to normalize and cross-validate, resulting in a score on a five-point scale on sentiment and permitting ease/risk.
When using the map, developers can zoom in with the company’s “Site Scout” on specific locations to gather far more information. For example, Site Scout offers not only public sentiment in the specific location, but also provides details on regulatory factors, names and contact information of key stakeholders and tools to continue monitoring evolving narratives for potential new risk signals.
After analyzing a location, the platform offers a feasibility assessment that runs from “very unfavorable” to “very favorable,” followed by a narrative of what that assessment is based on.
Jeremy Solomon, president and founder of Learnewable, told
pv magazine USA
that while AI gets a bad rap for providing false information, the company has found that by using multiple AI models it has learned how to minimize false information.
In addition to the web scraper and web tracker tools that continually monitor social media including Facebook and Nextdoor, Site Scout also has an audio and video tool that developers can use to download the text of city council, planning board or other meetings that are posted to YouTube. Called “Audio Insight,” the tool identifies stakeholders and summarizes their point of view. A proprietary algorithm, developed with a psychologist and after interviewing over 100 developers about their needs, then categorizes the stakeholders according to their potential influence.
Solomon referred to the algorithm as “the secret sauce,” which he said sets Site Scout apart. “Other offerings map sentiment, but we identify stakeholders,” he concluded.
Site Scout covers more than 3,000 counties in the U.S., providing color-coded maps and prioritized locations, as shown above. Solomon noted that by using these tools, the developer doesn’t need to hire a consultant, and the user owns the data that’s generated.
Learnewable was founded in 2023 by Solomon to develop an intuitive, AI-driven platform designed to simplify and accelerate the site selection process. The company initially focused on solar permitting but has added wind and battery storage as it continues to refine the platform.

title: Moldova simplifies rules governing solar, heat pumps, storage systems - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
Legislative changes in Moldova allow solar panels, heat pumps and energy storage systems to be installed without a building permit or urban planning certificate under certain circumstances.
Patrick Jowett
24 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Energy Storage
Heat pumps
Residential
The Parliament of Moldova has adopted legislative changes to make it quicker for individuals and companies to install solar panels, storage systems and heat pumps.
The updated legislation is designed to eliminate administrative barriers hindering the development of renewable energy projects and modernization of energy infrastructure while reducing time and costs, according to an update published by the country’s Ministry of Energy.
Under the changes, urban planning certificates and building permits are no longer required for the solar panels, heat pumps and any related infrastructure installed on the roof and facades of buildings, residential blocks and individual houses.
Energy storage systems that are located in photovoltaic parks, or within other existing or under construction energy infrastructures, can also be installed without an urban planning certificate or building permit.
The new law also reduces the project documentation required for these installations and simplifies urban planning procedures for projects located outside built-up areas, while introducing timelines for when a detailed urban plan is required.
The legislation also maintains measures to protect cultural heritage, with approvals from authorities still required in historical and protected areas and the installation of solar panels on individual historical monuments still prohibited.
The changes were promoted by Moldova’s Ministry of Energy and the Ministry of Infrastructure and Regional Development.
The two departments say the legislative amendments are aiming to create a modern regulatory framework that facilitates the development of energy infrastructure and contributes to strengthening Moldova’s energy security without compromising standards regarding construction safety, environmental protection and cultural heritage preservation.
Moldova had a record year for solar deployment in 2025, installing
and taking total capacity to 710 MW. By the end of last year, the country had deployed 980 MW of renewables.

title: Very-low-bandgap thermophotovoltaics for operation at higher temperatures - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
French researchers have developed very-low-bandgap thermophotovoltaic cells with a barrier structure designed to suppress dark current and enable operation at higher temperatures. The cells showed more than tenfold improved performance over conventional devices at temperatures above 150 K, with a photovoltaic effect observed up to 273 K.
Lior Kahana
24 Aug 2026
Research & Development
Cells & modules
Energy Storage
Researchers in France have developed very-low-bandgap thermophotovoltaic (TPV) cells featuring a barrier layer designed to suppress dark current. TPV, not to be confused with photovoltaic-thermal (PVT) technology, converts infrared (IR) radiation from heat sources directly into electricity using PV cells. Potential applications include thermal energy storage and the conversion of industrial process heat into electricity.
The technology has attracted scientific interest for decades because it can potentially capture a broader portion of the solar spectrum and has the technical potential to exceed the Shockley-Queisser limit of conventional photovoltaics. However, efficiencies reported to date have been too low for commercial viability, as TPV devices continue to suffer from optical and thermal losses.
“Our work reports on the first fabrication and characterization of a very-low-bandgap TPV cell (0.23 eV at 200 K), made of an indium arsenide/indium arsenide antimonide (InAs/InAsSb) type-II superlattice absorber, which is the material now widely used for photodetectors,” corresponding author Rodolphe Vaillon told
pv magazine
. “In other words, we have transformed an IR photodetector into a TPV cell, capable of operating at higher temperatures than those usual for IR photodetectors.”
Vaillon added that materials and structures used in IR photodetectors, such as InAs/InAsSb type-II superlattice barrier structures, appear to be good candidates for TPV energy conversion. “We show that the barrier structure is performing better than the standard p-intrinsic-n (PIN) structure at operating temperatures larger than 150 K. A photovoltaic effect is even observed at room temperature,” he said.
Very-low-bandgap TPV cells are suited to converting lower-energy infrared radiation, making them potentially useful for lower-temperature heat sources while also helping to maximize power generation. Their main drawback, however, is high dark current – unwanted electrical current that flows through a cell even in the absence of incoming radiation – which reduces voltage and power output.
High dark current typically requires very-low-bandgap cells to operate at cryogenic temperatures, such as around 77 K (−196 C). To reduce this cooling requirement, the researchers introduced an aluminum arsenide antimonide (AlAsSb) barrier layer. The barrier creates a band offset that restricts unwanted carrier flow through the device and suppresses surface-current leakage, thereby reducing dark current and enabling the cell to maintain better performance at higher operating temperatures.
The researchers fabricated two InAs/InAsSb type-II superlattice TPV cell designs: a conventional PIN structure used as a reference and a barrier structure incorporating a 200 nm AlAsSb layer. They processed the wafers into both small “micro” mesa cells and 1 × 1 cm² “macro” cells using metallization and wet etching. The micro cells also underwent sidewall passivation and received dielectric coatings.
The researchers characterized the grown layers using high-resolution X-ray diffraction, atomic force microscopy and photoluminescence measurements, while the finished devices underwent temperature-dependent current-voltage and dark-current testing. They then measured photovoltaic performance under infrared radiation from an 800 C thermal emitter positioned 14 cm from the cells.
“Once processed, the cells exposed to an 800 C emitter displayed improved performance by more than tenfold when compared to standard PIN ones (for temperatures above 150 K),” the researchers said. “The barrier layer, specific to this cell design, was also found to contribute greatly to the suppression of surface current leaking when associated with a passivation step (sulfuration).”
At a cell temperature of 123 K (−150 C), the barrier cells recorded open-circuit voltages of around 23 mV and fill factors of about 0.2, although one measurement produced an open-circuit voltage of 0.15 V. The researchers also demonstrated that a passivated barrier micro cell continued to exhibit a photovoltaic effect at 273 K (around 0 C), with an open-circuit voltage of about 75 mV.
“The fabrication process is robust, but improvements could still be expected by working on the characterization setup (especially the view factor) or by increasing the absorber bandgap to see how it affects the dark current,” the researchers concluded.
The results were presented in “
Fabrication and characterization of very-low bandgap InAs/InAsSb thermophotovoltaic cells
,” published in
Solar Energy Materials and Solar Cells
. Researchers from the
French National Centre for Scientific Research (CNRS)
University of Montpellier
, the University of Orléans, and the
University of Toulouse
contributed to the study.

title: Researchers use virtual reality to increase understanding of agrivoltaics - pv magazine Global
content:
Research & Development
Research from Denmark finds using immersive virtual reality can help citizens understand the dual-use logic of agrivoltaics. Participants in the research evaluated agrivoltaics as greener, more innovative and at least as acceptable as conventional solar parks.
Patrick Jowett
24 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Research & Development
Highlights
Using virtual reality (VR) to show citizens how future agrivoltaics projects will look and work can help increase understanding and acceptance, new research has found.
A research team at Aarhus University in Denmark used immersive virtual reality to examine how citizens evaluate agrivoltaic systems in comparison to conventional solar parks. Their findings are presented in the research paper
Cognitive and affective reasoning about agrivoltaics: The influence of experiential engagement on perceived purpose and acceptance intentions
, available in the journal
Environmental Science & Policy.
The team used VR to show 102 participants three solar configurations – one conventional solar park, a vertical agrivoltaic system, and a horizontal agrivoltaic system – from two standardized viewpoints, one approximately 50 metres away and another 2-3 metres away.
Participants were video recorded during the VR experiment to capture how their evaluations unfolded during exposure to the visualisation, while a pre- and post-VR survey assessed changes in perceptions and acceptance across each installation type.
Gabriele Torma, Assistant Professor at Aarhus University, told
pv magazine
that most of the participants started with very little familiarity with agrivoltaics.
“At first, they mainly reacted to how the installations looked in the landscape. But as they moved from the distant to the close view and more of the agricultural function became visible, many began to view them differently – not simply as solar panels occupying farmland, but as a way of using the same land for both food and energy production,” Torma explained.
Findings in the research paper highlight that agrivoltaics were evaluated more favorably than solar parks once participants fully understood the dual food–energy use the technology allows.
A quantitative analysis found agrivoltaics were rated substantially higher than conventional solar parks on compatibility with agriculture, environmental friendliness and innovativeness, according to additional analysis from the paper, but acceptance intentions were similarly high across all installation types, leading the paper to explain that unfamiliarity did not translate into lower stated local acceptance after experiential engagement.
Torma also told
pv magazine
the practical message from the research was that citizens and stakeholders need opportunities to understand what an unfamiliar technology will actually look like and how it is intended to work.
“VR, visualisations or site demonstrations can make both the visual impact and the functional logic of agrivoltaics more tangible, supporting a more informed discussion of benefits, trade-offs and design choices before projects are finalised,” she explained.
Torma added that one important limitation from the research was that all installations in the VR study were approximately one hectare.
“Some participants explicitly indicated that the relatively modest scale mattered to their evaluation, so we would not assume that the same findings necessarily apply to much larger installations,” she explained. “Design and scale still matter, and local context also needs to be considered, so these tools should support dialogue rather than be seen as a way of persuading communities to accept a project”.
Analysis from the research paper adds that the findings offer policy implications for the governance of agrivoltaics, including an implication that formal consultations could be complemented by experimental tools that allow stakeholders to engage directly with the functional logic behind these such systems.
“Deployed before concrete project proposals are finalized, such tools should be understood as complements to formal planning processes, supporting transparent dialogue and helping clarify trade-offs without presupposing agreement or acceptance,” the paper suggests.
It adds that as participants in the study had more informed evaluations of agrivoltaics once they could experience and interpret the system’s functional logic directly, the findings also have implications for social acceptance and land-use governance.
“In contexts where open-space solar development raises concerns about agricultural land conversion or local acceptance, agrivoltaics may offer a socially relevant complement to conventional solar parks, provided that continued agricultural activity remains visible and practically viable,” the paper says.
“While our findings do not speak to agronomic performance directly, the perceived credibility of continued farming was central to public evaluation. Agronomic feasibility, including crop compatibility, machinery access, yield expectations, and land-use efficiency, should therefore be communicated tangibly during planning and consultation.”
Torma added that the VR used in the study is available as freeware for non-commercial use through the
HyPErFarm project

title: India adds 3 GW of open-access solar in Q2 - pv magazine Global
content:
Applications & Installations
India added a record 3 GW of open-access solar capacity in the second quarter of 2026, taking cumulative installations to 36 GW. First-half additions reached nearly 6 GW, up 42% year on year, driven by strong C&I demand and regulatory deadlines.
Uma Gupta
24 Aug 2026
Applications & Installations
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
India added 3 GW of open-access solar capacity in the second quarter of 2026, marking the highest quarterly addition on record, according to Mercom India’s newly released Q2 & 1H 2026 India Solar Open Access Market Report.
In India, open-access solar allows commercial and industrial (C&I) consumers to procure electricity from off-site solar projects through the transmission and distribution network, rather than relying solely on their local distribution companies. Power is typically supplied under third-party power purchase agreements (PPAs) or captive and group-captive arrangements, with project economics determined by factors including state-level open-access regulations, grid charges, banking provisions and applicable surcharges.
The report also reveals that open-access installations rose 10% quarter on quarter, with Rajasthan accounting for 25% of capacity additions during the quarter.
Solar open-access additions reached nearly 6 GW in the first half of 2026, up 42% year on year from 4 GW in the same period of 2025.
Mercom India said installation activity during the first half of the year was influenced by regulatory deadlines and changing market conditions. Developers accelerated procurement and project commissioning ahead of the phased reduction of the interstate transmission system (ISTS) charge waiver and the implementation of sourcing requirements under the Approved List of Models and Manufacturers (ALMM) List-II.
The ALMM List-II requirements for open-access projects were subsequently deferred until the end of 2026. However, the extension came after the original deadline had passed, by which time many developers had already brought forward procurement and commissioning schedules.
“The record installations and a large pipeline demonstrate the strength of underlying demand from commercial and industrial consumers. However, rising project costs, transmission constraints, changing banking and open access regulations, and domestic sourcing requirements are putting pressure on project economics,” said Priya Sanjay, managing director at Mercom India.
“The opportunity remains significant, but growth will increasingly depend on states providing predictable regulations and developers being able to deliver projects at tariffs that continue to offer meaningful savings to consumers,” she added.
India’s cumulative installed open-access solar capacity reached 36 GW at the end of June 2026. Karnataka led with a 21% share of cumulative capacity, followed by Rajasthan and Maharashtra, each with 16%.
The five leading states accounted for 77% of cumulative capacity, reflecting the market’s continued concentration in states with strong industrial electricity demand and established open-access frameworks.

title: Norway installs 43 MW of solar in January-July - pv magazine Global
content:
Markets & Policy
As Norway’s cumulative solar capacity moves closer to 1 GW, the country’s C&I market accounts for the majority of new installations while its residential market stalls.
Patrick Jowett
24 Aug 2026
Markets & Policy
Commercial & industrial
Highlights
Residential
Utility-scale
Norway added 43 MW of solar between January and July this year, according to provisional figures published by the Norwegian Water Resources and Energy Directorate (NVE), taking the country’s cumulative solar capacity to 964 MW by the end of last month.
Hassan Gholami, a senior consultant on solar and storage at Multiconsult, told
pv magazine
that while the 43 MW total could rise by roughly 10-15% as NVE continues to register installations from the previous months, this year’s market growth remains the slowest recorded since 2021.
Solar systems between 100 kW and 1 MW in size, most often deployed on commercial and industrial (C&I) rooftops, make up around 60% of this year’s installations to date.
Gholami said the clearest success in Norway’s solar market currently is that the C&I segment continues to function without direct subsidies.
“Installations for self-consumption are carrying the market as they remain the only bankable case,” he explained. “Commercial property, logistics and retail, agriculture and municipal buildings all have substantial daytime load, and with module prices where they are, avoiding the full delivered cost of electricity on every self-consumed kWh is enough to justify the investment without subsidy.”
Gholami predicted that the C&I share should hold and may even grow next year, when considering that commercial development cycles typically take between 9 and 18 months from decision making to commissioning.
In contrast, Norway’s residential solar market has effectively stalled, with around 2 MW across 172 PV systems installed in seven months, against roughly 1,200 new household systems registered across the whole of 2025.
Norway’s fixed electricity price for households, known as the Norgepris, has removed most of the residential payback case, Gholami said.
“Beyond that, there is still no minimum compensation for exported power, so production above self-consumption is fully exposed to low daytime summer prices and the cannibalisation effect, and financing costs remain high by European standards,” he added
Gholami said the residential market will not recover without a specific support measure such as a guaranteed minimum price for exported power, restored support from [government enterprise] Enova at a meaningful level, or VAT relief on installation.
He added that a study mandated by the Norwegian parliament into a guaranteed minimum price for building-mounted solar power exported to the grid is due to be completed this year.
“Views on the level vary: Before its collapse [leading residential supplier] Solcellespesialisten argued that a floor of NOK 0.50 ($0.054)/kWh would not be enough to restore the sector, and a representative proposal in March put NOK 1.00/kWh on the table,” Gholami explained. “Whether it lands is a separate question, but it is the first serious movement on the demand side in some years.”
While Norway’s utility-scale solar market remains in its relative infancy, Gholami told
pv magazine
projects are moving from licensing to construction. NVE licensed a 31.4 MW PV project in June, to be developed by Norwegian company Energeia in the municipality Østre Toten. It is the country’s second-larger project under development following a
46 MW agrivoltaic project
belonging to Energeia and Norwegian utility Eidsiva.
Norway is also approving its first co-located storage installations, Gholami added, with the 7 MW Furuseth solar plant approved to add a 5 MW/13.5 MWh battery, while Energeia and Eidsiva’s agrivoltaic project is set to integrate a 6 MW/12 MWh battery.
A licence-exemption threshold introduced last year, which means plants up to 10 MW now require approval from the host municipality rather than a licence from NVE, is also helping to shape the development pipeline for ground-mounted projects, Gholami explained. “In most cases this means a zoning process or a dispensation,” he said.
Gholami forecasts this year’s installations to land between 80 MW and 100 MW, compared to 132 MW in 2025 and 172 MW in 2024, but said the utility-scale market could change the picture quickly in coming years. “A single 20–30 MW park commissioned in one year adds more than half of current national annual deployment, so if two or three licensed projects reach commissioning in 2027–28 the annual figures become considerably larger,” he explained.
Away from installations, Gholami said Norway’s solar sector has lost capacity across the value chain. Following Solcellespesialisten’s bankruptcy in December, solar energy companies Sesol and Solintegra AS have since gone into bankruptcy proceedings. “Beyond the job losses, this is a loss of trained installation capacity, and it leaves customers holding manufacturer warranties but no installer warranty,” Gholami added. “Rebuilding that capacity will take longer than rebuilding demand.”
Regulatory changes brought into effect in Norway this year include
energy sharing agreements
for businesses and a new connection obligation which requires local distribution companies to be responsible for building the final connection for new power plants connecting at up to and including 22 kV, rather than requiring the developer to apply to NVE for a separate gird licene for the line.
“Both are useful, but both build pipelines rather than deliver megawatts in the same year,” Gholami said.
During this year’s Intersolar,
pv magazine
spoke to Mulitconsult’s Mette Kristine Kanestrøm about the
recent developments
in Norway’s solar and storage sectors.
